stimulus.text: "That whereas your poor and humble petitioner being condemned to die do humbly beg of you to take it into your judicious and pious considerations.... I petition to your honours not for my own life for I know I must die and my appointed time is set but the Lord he knows it is that if it be possible no more innocent blood may be shed." — Mary Easty, petition from Salem jail, September 1692 (abridged; spelling modernized).
stimulus.source_note: Mary Easty, petition to Governor Phipps and the Salem court, September 1692; public domain.

rationales.general:
1. Ask who is speaking. A condemned woman, writing from jail, days from the gallows.
2. Ask what she asks for. Not her own life — she knows she must die — but that no more innocent blood be shed.
3. Ask what a historian gains. The voice of the accused, which the court records never preserve.
4. Rule out the rest. No girls testify here, no imperial policy, no judge's reasoning.
Remember: a petition from the condemned is the accused's side of the story — the one voice the trial record leaves out.
rationales.B: Easty writes as the condemned: she accepts that she must die and pleads instead that no more innocent blood be shed, showing both her terror and her charity toward fellow prisoners facing the same fate. The petition preserves the victim's voice — what it felt like to be accused — which the judges' records and the accusers' testimony never give. Background: Easty was hanged on September 22, 1692, one of the nineteen hanged at Salem. The other options name voices the petition does not contain.
rationales.A: The petition is not the afflicted girls' testimony; Easty writes from the other side, as one of the accused.
rationales.C: The petition reveals nothing about English imperial policy; it is a personal plea from a Salem jail cell.
rationales.D: The petition is not the judges' legal reasoning; it is the accused's response to that reasoning.
